cells.tense: You're in the middle of learning out loud, and you know it.
cells.ask: Write one page tonight about the thing you understand least. Stop when you catch yourself pretending, and leave it until morning.
cells.core:
The questions come before they're rehearsed, and you can hear yourself adjust mid-sentence when a word lands wrong. That's learning out loud, and it's steady — curiosity with its hands on the actual thing, not a performance of it. You sit with someone who knows more and ask the second question, the one past the easy one, and the asking is how the room opens.

The light you actually want doesn't need defending this week and doesn't need a name. But it goes quiet when you treat it as settled, and you have been treating it as settled. Keep one open question attached to it in plain words, and let it stay unfinished enough to pull. What you're moving toward stays alive the way anything alive stays alive — by being slightly out of reach.
cells.sheetLine: You're learning out loud, and the questions need no rehearsal.
cells.verb: learning out loud, asking toward what is not yet known
cells.place: pointed at the light you actually want, an aim you don't have to defend

cells.tense: You're racing toward a version of knowing that hasn't arrived yet.
cells.ask: Say one true sentence out loud to nobody. Then leave the rest of the thought unfinished until tomorrow, without rehearsing the ending.
cells.core:
You're learning ahead — running the conversation before it happens, sorting someone's argument one half-sentence early. The wheels spin clean, but they've left the present, which is the only place the light you're aimed at actually reaches you.

When questions grip the future like that, effort won't slow you down. Something else has to lead: finishing a small thing and letting it show, so what you make carries a little radiance on its own. That shine comes from work that reached its end, not from work still rehearsing. Pick something small enough to complete and let it be visible while it's still plain.

cells.tense: You're standing at a door you won't walk through, and you won't say so.
cells.ask: Ask one question you can't answer, out loud, to one person. Then let their answer sit for the rest of the day without fixing it.
cells.core:
Going well here looks like this: a question forms and you say it in the room it belongs to, and the answer, even a bad one, moves you. You don't flinch at the pause after asking, and you don't need the whole shape of the reply before you open your mouth. You know what you want and you follow it out loud, and the following is what keeps it lit.

What's actually happening is narrower. The questions still form; they just don't come out. You keep waiting for one you can already answer, and a question you can already answer isn't a question. So the light stays theoretical, and the aim stays on paper, and the days go by.
cells.sheetLine: You have a question in you that you've stopped asking.

cells.tense: You're drawing conclusions and calling the drawing a hunch.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're certain of, out loud, to someone. Then say how you got there in the next sentence, plainly, without softening it.
cells.core:
It looks like this when it's working: you say what you notice and the room adjusts — not because you pushed, but because what you said was right and you said it plainly. People lean in. You can tell which way the conversation is going before it turns, and you don't pretend otherwise, and it gets used.

What happens instead: you still see it, but when it lands you call it a hunch or a feeling or luck. Calling it a hunch is a kind of fairness, and that fairness keeps everything even. Even isn't accurate. Give the credit back to the one who saw it, and the next thing you notice will have somewhere to go.
cells.sheetLine: You've already seen it. You're still calling it a hunch.
